初學時先將邦哥鼓夾於雙腿間，右利手者把較大的陰鼓放右、較小的陽鼓放左；以手指與手: At the start, hold the bongo between the knees: a right-handed player puts the larger hembra on the right and the smaller macho on the left, and strikes the edge of the head with fingers and palm. For the basics, first practise the continuous eight-stroke pattern, then separately the finger stroke on the head, the palm stroke on the head, the press after the stroke, the thumb press with a stroke on the other drum, and the rim stroke. In classical or stage settings the drums can be set on a stand and struck with sticks or mallets.

邦哥鼓主要見於古巴頌樂與騷薩節奏組，常與康加鼓、蒂姆巴爾鼓並用，演奏者以雙手敲出: The bongo is heard mainly in the rhythm section of the Cuban son and salsa, often with congas and timbales, the player beating the continuous eight-beat "martillo" pattern with both hands and adding improvised fills. It is also used in the nengón and changüí of eastern Cuba, and later in bachata and Latin rock. In classical music it may be set on a stand and played with sticks or soft mallets, as in Varèse's Ionisation, Boulez's Le Marteau sans maître, Fortner's In seinem Garten liebt Don Perlimplín Belisa and Reich's Drumming.
邦哥鼓為兩只不同大小、底部開放的單皮鼓以木橋相連，屬膜鳴樂器。陰鼓（hembra: The bongo is two single-headed drums of different sizes, open at the bottom and joined by a wooden bridge, classed as a membranophone. The hembra is the larger, the macho the smaller, and the two together give high and low notes; the instrument as a whole is higher than the conga, though the traditional bongó de monte is lower. The tension of the heads can be adjusted, in modern drums usually with iron rings and nuts, traditionally by fire or water. It is played with the fingers on the rim and the palm on the head, and the pitch can be damped with the thumb or by pressing after the stroke; on the bongó de monte the fingers are rubbed on the head to make a glissando. There is no fixed absolute pitch, and notation mostly shows only the combination of high and low; the sources do not clearly record how the volume is controlled.
邦哥鼓為非裔古巴打擊樂器，最早見於19世紀末古巴東部奧連特省，用於內貢、昌圭與後: The bongo is an Afro-Cuban percussion instrument, first found at the end of the nineteenth century in Oriente province in eastern Cuba, used in the nengón, the changüí and later the Cuban son. The larger mountain bongo is seen as the ancestor of the smaller bongo, and oral tradition also holds that it was adapted from paired bokú drums. Early heads were fixed with nails and tuned with fire, later with metal screws. In the 1910s the smaller bongo spread through Cuba with the son, in the 1930s it reached the music halls of the eastern United States, and in the 1940s it shared the stage with the conga and came into contact with jazz and other genres. In the second half of the twentieth century its use extended to bachata, Latin rock and other kinds of music.
邦哥鼓的鼓身與連接橋通常為木製，玻璃纖維亦常見；鼓面傳統多用小牛皮，早期以金屬釘: The bongo's shells and the bridge between them are usually wooden, with fibreglass also common; the heads are traditionally calfskin and were fixed with metal nails early on, needing fire, water or tapping to adjust the tension, while modern drums tune with steel hardware. Some sources also record that early drums were fired from clay with the skin edge lashed with rope, and that modern heads use a fibre film fixed by iron rings or a frame and tuned with nuts and a key.
邦哥鼓（西班牙語 bongó）是非洲古巴打擊樂器，由一大一小兩個底部開放手鼓以木: The bongo (Spanish bongó) is an Afro-Cuban percussion instrument made of one large and one small open-bottomed hand drum joined by a wooden bridge, the larger called hembra and the smaller macho. It is mostly played with both hands and usually held between the knees; in classical settings sticks may be used or the drums set on a stand. Its Hornbostel–Sachs number is 211.251.2. Bongo players are common in the rhythm section of Cuban son and salsa ensembles, and the drum also appears in orchestras and bands.
